```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"
)
```

```{r setup}
library(sedacore)
```

This walks through the same workflow the Shiny app (`run_sedacore_app()`)
wires together interactively -- map, retrieve from PANGAEA, find
neighbours, harmonize, interpolate, export -- but calling the underlying
functions directly from a script. Every step here also works as a
building block for a larger, scripted metaanalysis pipeline that doesn't
need the app at all.

The steps that call the live PANGAEA API are shown but not run here (to
keep this vignette buildable offline and independent of PANGAEA's
uptime); everything else runs for real against the package's bundled
synthetic example file.

## 1. Map your cores

The input is one row per subsample -- see `vignette("sedacore")`'s
package README section "Input format" for the full column reference.
Only `core_id`, `latitude`, `longitude`, and `depth_cm` are required;
`as_sample_registry()` maps your raw column names onto that standardized
shape.

```{r}
raw <- readr::read_tsv(
  system.file("extdata", "example_core_metadata.tsv", package = "sedacore"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

sr <- as_sample_registry(raw)
cr <- collapse_to_core_registry(sr)
cr[, c("core_id", "latitude", "longitude", "n_samples", "depth_min_cm", "depth_max_cm")]
```

`collapse_to_core_registry()` derives one row per physical core from the
per-sample table -- the unit the map, PANGAEA retrieval, and neighbour
search all operate on.

```{r, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4}
plot_core_map(cr)
```

`leaflet_core_map(cr)` gives the same thing as an interactive widget
(what the app's "Map" tab uses); omitted here since it doesn't render in
a static vignette.

## 2. Retrieve matching PANGAEA datasets

`pg_search_cores()` searches PANGAEA near a core's coordinates;
`pg_fetch_dataset()` retrieves a candidate DOI's actual data.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
candidates <- pg_search_cores(cr[cr$core_id == "EXCORE1-1", ], count = 20)
candidates[, c("doi", "score", "citation")]

fetched <- pg_fetch_dataset(candidates$doi[1])
```

## 3. Harmonize into one long table

`harmonize_columns()` pivots a raw wide PANGAEA table into the package's
long `param_long` format, matching column names against
`inst/extdata/column_synonyms.csv`. Every numeric column is kept even if
it isn't yet in that table (tagged `parameter_group = "uncategorized"`
instead of dropped) -- PANGAEA's column naming is too inconsistent
across datasets to risk silently losing real measurements.

```{r}
# A small stand-in for `fetched$data[[1]]` above, shaped like a real
# PANGAEA isotope table, so this step runs offline in the vignette.
raw_pangaea_table <- tibble::tibble(
  `Depth sed [m]` = c(0.03, 0.08, 0.13, 0.18),
  `G. inflata δ18O [‰ PDB]` = c(1.46, 1.12, 0.91, 0.85),
  `TOC [%]` = c(2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 1.9)
)

h <- harmonize_columns(raw_pangaea_table, core_id = "EXCORE1-1", doi = "10.1594/PANGAEA.218244")
h
```

## 4. Find neighbouring cores

Some cores have no PANGAEA data of their own; `find_neighbours()`
searches within a radius and ranks results GeoB/IODP-first, most-recent
first (PANGAEA's own search relevance isn't distance-aware).

```{r, eval = FALSE}
neighbours <- find_neighbours(cr, "EXCORE1-1", radius_km = 50, count = 50)
neighbours[, c("neighbour_core_id", "neighbour_doi", "distance_km", "source_program")]
```

## 5. Depth-match against your sample depths

`report_depth_coverage()` matches (or linearly interpolates) harmonized
measurements onto a set of target depths -- e.g. sedaDNA sample
depths -- and always returns one row per (depth, parameter) combination,
even when nothing was found there, flagged via `match_status`. That
makes a genuine coverage gap (e.g. retrieved data at 300-1000 cm when
your samples are at 40-200 cm) visible instead of silently returning
nothing.

```{r}
sample_depths <- c(3, 8, 15)
report_depth_coverage(h, sample_depths)
```

## 6. Check a fixed measurement checklist

`check_target_measurements()` cross-references a short list of
parameters of particular interest (`inst/extdata/target_measurements.csv`
-- TOC, TN, CaCO3, age model, ... edit that file to change the list)
against what's actually been retrieved for a core, so it's clear at a
glance what's still missing.

```{r}
check_target_measurements(h, "EXCORE1-1")
```

## 7. Export

```{r, eval = FALSE}
write_harmonized_tsv(h, "harmonized.tsv")
```

## Or just use the app

Everything above is exactly what `run_sedacore_app()` wires together
into an interactive Shiny app -- map on one side, retrieve/harmonize/
interpolate/export controls on the other. Reach for the functions
directly when scripting a larger pipeline; reach for the app for
interactive, exploratory work on one core metadata file at a time.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
run_sedacore_app()
```
